We use will/won't with the if-clause to describe conditions that are likely to come true. Look at the sentence below:

Example: If you come early enough, (then) you will get better seats.

In the example above, the first part of the sentence “ If you come early enough” describes a condition. The result or outcome is expressed by the second part of the sentence “you will get better seats.”

The “result clause” is always true, whenever the “condition” is true. If, on the other hand, the condition is not met, then the result will also not be realized.

We also use will/won't with the If clause when we want to communicate a polite request, strong disapproval or outright refusal. Look at the examples below:

Adverb clauses can put a condition on an action. You use the conjunctions if, whether, provided that and unless to introduce the condition.

If you cross the street on a red light, you will get run over.
You will get fat, if you eat too much candy.
Unless you tell me where the party is, I won't be able to attend.
Provided you do your work, everything will work out in the end.

When you use the unreal conditional you can skip “if ”.

images.text:
Candice: Hi, Amy. If you'll just take a seat right there, I'll be with you ... now, what's on your mind?
Amy: I've been thinking. I know that in the short term we're helping out, but are we really providing a long-term solution for these people?
Candice: Of course we are ...
Amy: I guess I'm just having a bit of an ethical dilemma. I mean, so long as we keep sending care packages, we won't see any lasting progress.

Candice: That's exactly why we don't send care packages. We realized a long time ago that unless we help the local people through education, we won't see any real change.
Amy: Isn't it a bit arrogant to think that they even need our help? I mean, if we don't help, they'll just suffer. Is that the idea?
Candice: Not at all. The effects of colonization, years of poor governance, and civil war have taken their toll. It's our responsibility to help undo some of the mistakes of the past.
Amy: But how do we know that it's working?

Candice: If you'll just hold on a second, I'll dig up the numbers ... here they are. You see? In our community, employment is up and the infection rate is down. Provided that we focus on education, I am sure we will continue to see incremental improvements.
Amy: I guess I'm just focused on this news report I heard about disaster relief. It showed so much corruption and misappropriation of funds.
Candice: Those NGOs are outdated. If they won't change, then there's really nothing we can do about it. We've got to focus on ourselves.
Amy: I agree. In the interest of transparency, why don't convince the director to post all of our cash flow online.
Candice: What a great idea! If he won't do it, I will.
